passages.text: Sleep, Stress, Circadian Rhythm, and Diet in Pediatric Disorders of Gut-Brain Interaction: A Narrative Review

Pediatric disorders of gut-brain interaction (DGBIs) comprise chronic or recurrent symptom-based gastrointestinal conditions that cannot be fully explained by identifiable structural, biochemical, or organic abnormalities after appropriate clinical evaluation. <sentence_start/>The term DGBI is used throughout this review in accordance with current terminology, whereas the historical term “functional gastrointestinal disorders” (FGIDs) is retained only when referring to studies that used earlier Rome classifications. <sentence_start/>This review examines the impact of four modifiable factors-sleep, psychological stress, circadian rhythm, and diet-on their development and severity in children and adolescents. <sentence_start/>Relevant literature was identified through PubMed, with emphasis on recent pediatric studies, systematic reviews, and meta-analyses. <sentence_start/>Sleep disturbances are associated with greater abdominal pain, functional disability, and impaired daytime functioning. <sentence_start/>Stress may exacerbate symptoms through hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis activation, autonomic imbalance, altered motility, and visceral hypersensitivity. <sentence_start/>Circadian disruption may affect gastrointestinal motility, barrier function, enteroendocrine signaling, and microbial rhythmicity, although pediatric evidence remains limited. <sentence_start/>Diet influences fermentation, microbiota, intestinal permeability, and symptom expression, with regular meals, adequate hydration, and appropriate fiber intake representing important initial measures. <sentence_start/>These factors interact bidirectionally through shared neuroendocrine, autonomic, immune, and microbial pathways. <sentence_start/>Clinical management should therefore adopt a biopsychosocial, multidisciplinary approach combining symptom management with modification of sleep, stress, circadian habits, and dietary patterns. <sentence_start/>Further prospective pediatric studies are needed to clarify causality and support personalized interventions.
1. Characteristics of Functional Gastrointestinal Disorders in Children

Pediatric functional gastrointestinal disorders (FGIDs), increasingly referred to as “disorders of gut-brain interaction” (DGBIs), comprise chronic or recurrent symptom-based gastrointestinal conditions that cannot be fully explained by identifiable structural, biochemical, or organic abnormalities after appropriate clinical evaluation [<citation rid="B1-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.14218/JTG.2023.00075" count="1">1</citation>,<citation rid="B2-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fped.2023.1283389" pmid="38433954" pmcid="PMC10904537" count="1">2</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The Rome IV criteria provided an age-specific symptom-based framework that distinguished disorders of infancy and early childhood from those occurring in older children and adolescents [<citation rid="B3-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.5056/jnm16214" pmid="28274109" pmcid="PMC5383110" count="1">3</citation>,<citation rid="B4-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1053/j.gastro.2016.02.032" pmid="27144617" count="1">4</citation>,<citation rid="B5-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1053/j.gastro.2016.02.015" pmid="27144632" count="1">5</citation>,<citation rid="B6-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.5223/pghn.2017.20.1.1" pmid="28401050" pmcid="PMC5385301" count="1">6</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In 2026, the Rome V criteria introduced an updated pediatric framework. <sentence_start/>Among the changes most relevant to this review, pediatric DGBIs are now organized predominantly according to gastrointestinal region and symptom pattern rather than the previous age-based subdivision. <sentence_start/>Rome V also revised the diagnostic criteria for several disorders discussed in this review, including irritable bowel syndrome and functional constipation, and expanded the classification of upper gastrointestinal DGBIs, including chronic nausea syndrome and functional dyspepsia [<citation rid="B7-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1053/j.gastro.2026.01.039" pmid="41713704" pmcid="PMC13202739" count="1">7</citation>,<citation rid="B8-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1053/j.gastro.2026.01.036" pmid="41713707" count="1">8</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Their pathophysiology is multifactorial and involves altered gastrointestinal motility, visceral hypersensitivity, mucosal and immune mechanisms, gut microbiota alterations, and altered central processing of visceral signals [<citation rid="B4-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1053/j.gastro.2016.02.032" pmid="27144617" count="1">4</citation>,<citation rid="B9-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/gidisord6010021" count="1">9</citation>,<citation rid="B10-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fped.2022.805466" pmid="35252059" pmcid="PMC8888932" count="1">10</citation>].

Rather than providing an exhaustive review of pediatric DGBIs, the present review focuses primarily on pain-predominant disorders in school-aged children and adolescents, particularly irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), functional dyspepsia (FD), and functional abdominal pain not otherwise specified (FAP-NOS), together with nausea-related DGBIs and functional constipation, as these are the entities most directly represented in the pediatric evidence discussed below [<citation rid="B5-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1053/j.gastro.2016.02.015" pmid="27144632" count="1">5</citation>,<citation rid="B6-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.5223/pghn.2017.20.1.1" pmid="28401050" pmcid="PMC5385301" count="1">6</citation>,<citation rid="B7-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1053/j.gastro.2026.01.039" pmid="41713704" pmcid="PMC13202739" count="1">7</citation>,<citation rid="B8-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1053/j.gastro.2026.01.036" pmid="41713707" count="1">8</citation>,<citation rid="B11-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/jcm10215087" pmid="34768604" pmcid="PMC8585107" count="1">11</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Most studies included in this review predate Rome V and therefore use Rome III or Rome IV definitions; their original diagnostic terminology is retained where necessary to accurately describe the populations studied. <sentence_start/>Abdominal migraine remains part of the Rome IV functional abdominal pain disorder spectrum but is not a major focus of this review.

Pediatric functional gastrointestinal disorders are common, although prevalence estimates vary according to the diagnostic criteria used, participants’ age, data collection methods, and geographical region. <sentence_start/>A systematic review based on the Rome IV criteria showed that these disorders affect a substantial proportion of children, including those under 4 years of age as well as children and adolescents aged 4-18 years [<citation rid="B11-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/jcm10215087" pmid="34768604" pmcid="PMC8585107" count="1">11</citation>]. <sentence_start/>A meta-analysis estimated the global prevalence of functional abdominal pain disorders at 13.5%, with higher rates among girls and considerable heterogeneity between studies [<citation rid="B12-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1371/journal.pone.0126982" pmid="25992621" pmcid="PMC4439136" count="1">12</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In a population-based study, Robin et al. reported that approximately one in four children and adolescents met the Rome IV criteria for at least one functional gastrointestinal disorder [<citation rid="B13-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.jpeds.2017.12.012" pmid="29398057" count="1">13</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Studies comparing Rome III and Rome IV further indicate that applying Rome IV may change and in some cases reduce prevalence estimates for individual diagnoses; this should be considered when interpreting epidemiological data [<citation rid="B14-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1177/2333794X211022265" pmcid="PMC8170292" pmid="34104704" count="1">14</citation>].

The clinical significance of these disorders extends beyond somatic symptoms alone. <sentence_start/>Children with DGBIs frequently experience impaired health-related quality of life, with the disease affecting physical activity, emotional functioning, family relationships, and daily participation in education [<citation rid="B15-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s11136-009-9583-y" pmid="20069377" pmcid="PMC2836462" count="1">15</citation>]. <sentence_start/>School absenteeism is an important indicator of disease burden, as children with functional gastrointestinal disorders may miss school more frequently because of their symptoms, while school avoidance may further exacerbate anxiety, activity limitation, and functional disability [<citation rid="B16-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fped.2024.1503783" pmid="39726527" pmcid="PMC11669597" count="1">16</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In clinical practice, symptom overlap and the risk of symptom persistence are also important considerations; therefore, both gastrointestinal symptoms and psychosocial factors should be incorporated into diagnostic and therapeutic approaches [<citation rid="B17-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fped.2025.1576698" pmid="40433476" pmcid="PMC12108103" count="1">17</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Although functional constipation is often regarded as a benign condition, it may result in abdominal pain, abdominal bloating, fecal incontinence, toilet avoidance, family distress, and impaired quality of life in affected children [<citation rid="B18-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1097/MPG.0000000000000266" pmid="24345831" count="1">18</citation>,<citation rid="B19-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3748/wjg.v29.i8.1261" pmid="36925458" pmcid="PMC10011959" count="1">19</citation>].

This review summarises the current state of knowledge regarding circadian rhythm-related functional disorders, dietary factors and behavioural phenomena such as stress, thereby providing a basis for further research into a holistic approach to this group of disorders.

In this review, the literature search done between march till august 2026 focused on the relationship between sleep, psychological stress, circadian rhythm, dietary habits, and functional gastrointestinal disorders in children and adolescents. <sentence_start/>Seventy-three relevant publications were identified primarily through searches of the PubMed database using combinations of keywords related to pediatric functional gastrointestinal disorders disorders of gut-brain interaction, sleep, stress, circadian rhythm, diet, and gastrointestinal symptoms. <sentence_start/>Original research articles, randomized controlled trials, systematic reviews, and meta-analyses were considered. <sentence_start/>Particular attention was given to recent studies and publications directly addressing pediatric populations, while older or adult and experimental studies were included when they provided important mechanistic or clinical context. <sentence_start/>Additional relevant references were identified from the bibliographies of selected publications.
2. <sentence_start/>Sleep and Its Impact on Gastrointestinal Symptoms

Sleep is a fundamental physiological process regulating neuroendocrine, immune, metabolic, and cognitive-emotional functions; therefore, its role in pediatric functional gastrointestinal disorders should be considered within the biopsychosocial model. <sentence_start/>Sleep is a multidimensional construct, and the terms used in pediatric DGBI studies should not be treated interchangeably. <sentence_start/>In this review, “sleep duration” refers to total sleep time, sleep quality encompasses subjective satisfaction, continuity, and sleep efficiency. <sentence_start/>“Sleep timing” refers to the timing and regularity of sleep onset and awakening in relation to the circadian cycle, and “insomnia symptoms” refer primarily to difficulties initiating or maintaining sleep accompanied by impaired daytime functioning. <sentence_start/>Pediatric DGBI studies frequently assess more than one of these domains or use composite sleep-disturbance scores, which complicates comparisons between studies [<citation rid="B38-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/jpepsy/jsad047" pmid="37515755" count="1">38</citation>,<citation rid="B42-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.2147/PHMT.S482343" pmcid="PMC11912920" pmid="40099110" count="1">42</citation>,<citation rid="B43-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/nmo.14992" pmid="39737536" pmcid="PMC11996607" count="1">43</citation>].

Schurman et al. demonstrated that clinically significant sleep problems were present in a substantial proportion of children with FGID and were associated with greater functional disability, primarily through increased physical symptom severity [<citation rid="B20-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/1471-230X-12-142" pmid="23067390" pmcid="PMC3527282" count="1">20</citation>]. <sentence_start/>A study by Jansen et al. confirmed that sleep disturbances in children with FGID are associated with greater daily abdominal pain severity and increased pain-related interference with the child’s daily activities [<citation rid="B21-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.5664/jcsm.9166" pmid="33590819" pmcid="PMC8314671" count="1">21</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Similar findings have been reported in adolescents with functional abdominal pain, in whom coexisting sleep disturbances are associated with greater pain severity and poorer daytime functioning [<citation rid="B39-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1080/15402002.2020.1781634" pmid="32573267" pmcid="PMC8063352" count="1">39</citation>]. <sentence_start/>More recent evidence supports these observations. <sentence_start/>A systematic review of 24 studies involving 110,864 children and adolescents found that pediatric patients with DGBIs experienced more sleep problems than healthy peers and that sleep disturbances were associated with worse pain, mood, and functional outcomes [<citation rid="B38-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/jpepsy/jsad047" pmid="37515755" count="1">38</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Although the included studies were heterogeneous and most were of moderate or weak methodological quality, the findings support the clinical relevance of sleep assessment in pediatric DGBIs [<citation rid="B38-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/jpepsy/jsad047" pmid="37515755" count="1">38</citation>].

The importance of sleep is also evident across specific disorder subtypes. <sentence_start/>In a study by Kim involving children with functional abdominal pain disorders, impaired sleep quality was common and was particularly pronounced among patients with irritable bowel syndrome [<citation rid="B40-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s41105-021-00342-9" pmcid="PMC10897639" pmid="38469067" count="1">40</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Colombo et al. demonstrated that, in children and adolescents with functional dyspepsia or IBS, the presence of heartburn co-occurs with sleep disturbances, anxiety, and depression. <sentence_start/>These findings suggest that the overlap of upper and lower gastrointestinal symptoms is more common among patients with a greater clinical and psychological burden [<citation rid="B41-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1097/MD.0000000000025426" pmid="33787652" pmcid="PMC8021315" count="1">41</citation>]. <sentence_start/>A review by Friesen et al. concluded that sleep disturbances are common in children and adolescents with chronic abdominal pain; however, the quality of the available evidence is limited by heterogeneity in sleep definitions, the predominance of cross-sectional studies, and the infrequent use of objective sleep assessment methods [<citation rid="B42-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.2147/PHMT.S482343" pmcid="PMC11912920" pmid="40099110" count="1">42</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Importantly, a 2025 scoping review of 32 studies reported sleep disturbance prevalence ranging from 19% to 75% among pediatric abdominal pain cohorts and concluded that the available evidence supports routine screening for sleep disturbances in youth with chronic abdominal pain [<citation rid="B42-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.2147/PHMT.S482343" pmcid="PMC11912920" pmid="40099110" count="1">42</citation>]. <sentence_start/>At the same time, the authors emphasized that the extent to which sleep-directed interventions improve abdominal pain and disability remains uncertain [<citation rid="B42-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.2147/PHMT.S482343" pmcid="PMC11912920" pmid="40099110" count="1">42</citation>].

Recent pediatric data further support the importance of distinguishing between specific sleep domains. <sentence_start/>In a school-based study of 120 adolescents, including 60 participants with FAPDs and 60 age- and sex-matched controls, youth with FAPDs reported significantly greater insomnia symptoms, general sleep disturbance, sleep-related impairment, and daytime sleepiness (<italic>p</italic> < 0.05 for these comparisons). <sentence_start/>Within the FAPD group, insomnia severity showed a moderate correlation with abdominal pain severity (r = 0.41, <italic>p</italic> < 0.01) [<citation rid="B43-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/nmo.14992" pmid="39737536" pmcid="PMC11996607" count="1">43</citation>]. <sentence_start/>These findings strengthen evidence for an association but remain cross-sectional and therefore do not establish the direction of causality. <sentence_start/>Importantly, recent objective data suggest that sleep abnormalities in pediatric DGBIs are not limited to subjective sleep complaints. <sentence_start/>In a 2026 case-control study using overnight polysomnography, children and adolescents with DGBIs demonstrated lower sleep efficiency after sleep onset, reduced NREM3 and REM sleep, and higher arousal and apnea-related indices than healthy controls [<citation rid="B50-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.sleep.2026.108907" pmid="41880878" pmcid="PMC13179843" count="1">50</citation>]. <sentence_start/>These findings provide objective evidence of altered sleep architecture in pediatric DGBIs, although the cross-sectional design does not establish whether these abnormalities contribute to gastrointestinal symptoms, result from them, or reflect shared underlying factors.

Several interconnected biological pathways may underlie the relationship between sleep and gastrointestinal symptoms. <sentence_start/>Sleep disturbance may influence pain processing through alterations in central pain modulation, emotional regulation, autonomic activity, and hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis function. <sentence_start/>Experimental and clinical evidence suggests that insufficient or fragmented sleep may increase pain sensitivity and reduce endogenous pain inhibition, potentially increasing the perception of visceral and somatic stimuli. <sentence_start/>Evidence from pediatric chronic pain populations, a broader category that includes chronic or functional abdominal pain as well as other chronic pain conditions, indicates that insufficient or disturbed sleep is associated with greater pain intensity, functional impairment, and internalizing symptoms [<citation rid="B51-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.cnur.2021.02.009" pmcid="PMC11756263" pmid="34023124" count="1">51</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Within pediatric functional abdominal pain specifically, sleep disturbance has likewise been associated with greater pain severity and poorer daytime functioning [<citation rid="B39-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1080/15402002.2020.1781634" pmid="32573267" pmcid="PMC8063352" count="1">39</citation>]. <sentence_start/>These relationships appear to be bidirectional, because pain may interfere with sleep, whereas disturbed sleep may increase pain vulnerability and functional impairment on the following day [<citation rid="B38-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/jpepsy/jsad047" pmid="37515755" count="1">38</citation>,<citation rid="B39-nutrients-18-02768" pmcid="PMC11912920" pmid="40099110" count="1">42</citation>,<citation rid="B51-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.cnur.2021.02.009" pmcid="PMC11756263" pmid="34023124" count="1">51</citation>].

The autonomic nervous system may represent an additional pathway linking sleep with gastrointestinal symptoms. <sentence_start/>Sleep disturbance may alter sympathetic and parasympathetic activity and increase physiological arousal, potentially affecting gastrointestinal motility and the perception of visceral stimuli. <sentence_start/>In children with functional abdominal pain and IBS, differences in autonomic regulation and sympathovagal balance have been associated with symptom severity and emotional status [<citation rid="B52-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.jpain.2012.02.007" pmid="22520688" pmcid="PMC3566525" count="1">52</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In children with pain-predominant FGID, associations between autonomic function and gastric motility have also been observed, further supporting the biological plausibility of interactions among sleep, stress, physiological arousal, and dyspeptic symptoms [<citation rid="B53-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3748/wjg.v25.i1.95" pmid="30643361" pmcid="PMC6328964" count="1">53</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Recent evidence provides additional support for this relationship. <sentence_start/>In a 2026 study of 156 children aged 7-12 years with abdominal pain-related DGBIs, heart rate variability measures were associated with selected sleep characteristics, with some associations differing between girls and boys [<citation rid="B54-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/nmo.70293" pmid="41873558" pmcid="PMC13010199" count="1">54</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Lower autonomic activity was also associated with sleep-disordered breathing in both sexes [<citation rid="B54-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/nmo.70293" pmid="41873558" pmcid="PMC13010199" count="1">54</citation>]. <sentence_start/>These findings suggest that autonomic regulation may contribute to the sleep-DGBI relationship; however, longitudinal studies are required to determine the direction and clinical significance of these associations.

Visceral hypersensitivity represents another potential mechanism contributing to abdominal pain. <sentence_start/>Anderson et al. evaluated experimental visceral sensitivity in 101 children aged 8-15 years with medically unexplained functional abdominal pain using the water load symptom provocation task (WL-SPT) [<citation rid="B55-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1097/MPG.0b013e3181653a6f" pmid="18728527" pmcid="PMC3101499" count="1">55</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Clinical gastrointestinal symptoms, functional disability, depressive symptoms, non-gastrointestinal symptoms, and pain-related efficacy beliefs were assessed at the initial clinical evaluation, whereas visceral sensitivity was assessed approximately two months later as the increase in gastrointestinal symptoms induced by the WL-SPT. <sentence_start/>More severe baseline gastrointestinal symptoms and greater functional disability were associated with significantly greater experimentally provoked gastrointestinal symptoms (<italic>p</italic> < 0.04), whereas greater problem-focused pain efficacy was associated with lower laboratory visceral sensitivity (<italic>p</italic> < 0.01) [<citation rid="B55-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1097/MPG.0b013e3181653a6f" pmid="18728527" pmcid="PMC3101499" count="1">55</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Depressive and non-gastrointestinal symptoms were not significantly associated with laboratory visceral sensitivity. <sentence_start/>These findings support an association between clinical gastrointestinal symptom burden and experimentally evoked visceral sensitivity; however, they do not demonstrate that sleep disturbance itself causes visceral hypersensitivity. <sentence_start/>Direct pediatric evidence linking sleep disturbance to experimentally measured visceral sensitivity therefore remains limited [<citation rid="B42-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.2147/PHMT.S482343" pmcid="PMC11912920" pmid="40099110" count="1">42</citation>,<citation rid="B51-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.cnur.2021.02.009" pmcid="PMC11756263" pmid="34023124" count="1">51</citation>,<citation rid="B55-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1097/MPG.0b013e3181653a6f" pmid="18728527" pmcid="PMC3101499" count="1">55</citation>].

The effects of sleep on specific symptoms, including abdominal pain, constipation, diarrhea, nausea, and appetite, are likely mediated through a combination of pain-related, autonomic, hormonal, and behavioral mechanisms. <sentence_start/>Poor sleep may exacerbate abdominal pain by lowering the pain threshold and increasing vigilance toward bodily sensations [<citation rid="B20-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/1471-230X-12-142" pmid="23067390" pmcid="PMC3527282" count="1">20</citation>,<citation rid="B21-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.5664/jcsm.9166" pmid="33590819" pmcid="PMC8314671" count="1">21</citation>,<citation rid="B39-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1080/15402002.2020.1781634" pmid="32573267" pmcid="PMC8063352" count="1">39</citation>,<citation rid="B51-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.cnur.2021.02.009" pmcid="PMC11756263" pmid="34023124" count="1">51</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In patients with IBS, sleep disturbances may coexist with either constipation or diarrhea; however, pediatric studies more consistently demonstrate an association between sleep and pain severity and functional impairment than with a specific bowel habit subtype [<citation rid="B38-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/jpepsy/jsad047" pmid="37515755" count="1">38</citation>,<citation rid="B40-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s41105-021-00342-9" pmcid="PMC10897639" pmid="38469067" count="1">40</citation>,<citation rid="B42-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.2147/PHMT.S482343" pmcid="PMC11912920" pmid="40099110" count="1">42</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In children with IBS, available evidence does not currently support a consistent sleep-related pattern for a particular stool phenotype [<citation rid="B40-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s41105-021-00342-9" pmcid="PMC10897639" pmid="38469067" count="1">40</citation>,<citation rid="B42-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.2147/PHMT.S482343" pmcid="PMC11912920" pmid="40099110" count="1">42</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Nausea, heartburn, and dyspeptic symptoms may further impair sleep, as has been observed in children with functional dyspepsia and IBS [<citation rid="B41-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1097/MD.0000000000025426" pmid="33787652" pmcid="PMC8021315" count="1">41</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Consequently, the relationship between sleep and gastrointestinal symptoms is likely reciprocal rather than unidirectional, with gastrointestinal symptoms potentially disrupting sleep while disturbed sleep may increase symptom burden and functional impairment [<citation rid="B38-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/jpepsy/jsad047" pmid="37515755" count="1">38</citation>,<citation rid="B39-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1080/15402002.2020.1781634" pmid="32573267" pmcid="PMC8063352" count="1">39</citation>,<citation rid="B42-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.2147/PHMT.S482343" pmcid="PMC11912920" pmid="40099110" count="1">42</citation>,<citation rid="B51-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.cnur.2021.02.009" pmcid="PMC11756263" pmid="34023124" count="1">51</citation>].

Sleep may also interact with gastrointestinal physiology through effects on motility, appetite regulation, circadian organization, and daily behavioral patterns. <sentence_start/>Irregular sleep schedules may coincide with irregular meal timing, evening eating, and other behavioral changes that can independently influence gastrointestinal function. <sentence_start/>These factors may be particularly relevant during childhood and adolescence, when sleep schedules are influenced by school demands, extracurricular activities, evening screen exposure, and social schedules. <sentence_start/>However, the current pediatric evidence does not allow the relative contribution of these factors to DGBI symptoms to be determined. <sentence_start/>Accordingly, these pathways should be considered biologically plausible contributors rather than established causal mechanisms.

These findings have practical implications for clinical assessment. <sentence_start/>The clinical evaluation of a child with an FGID should include questions regarding sleep duration, regularity of sleep onset, nocturnal awakenings, daytime sleepiness, evening screen use, and the impact of gastrointestinal symptoms on sleep [<citation rid="B20-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1186/1471-230X-12-142" pmid="23067390" pmcid="PMC3527282" count="1">20</citation>,<citation rid="B21-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.5664/jcsm.9166" pmid="33590819" pmcid="PMC8314671" count="1">21</citation>,<citation rid="B42-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.2147/PHMT.S482343" pmcid="PMC11912920" pmid="40099110" count="1">42</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Recent reviews support routine screening for sleep disturbances in children and adolescents with DGBIs or chronic abdominal pain, particularly given the high prevalence of sleep problems and their association with pain and functional impairment [<citation rid="B38-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/jpepsy/jsad047" pmid="37515755" count="1">38</citation>,<citation rid="B42-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.2147/PHMT.S482343" pmcid="PMC11912920" pmid="40099110" count="1">42</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Importantly, identification of sleep disturbance does not establish it as the primary cause of gastrointestinal symptoms; rather, it may identify a potentially modifiable factor contributing to symptom persistence and impaired daily functioning. <sentence_start/>The biological mechanisms potentially linking sleep with gastrointestinal symptoms are summarized schematically in Figure 1.

Whether improvement of sleep alone reduces gastrointestinal symptoms in children remains uncertain. <sentence_start/>The available pediatric literature predominantly evaluates associations between sleep characteristics and DGBI outcomes, and adequately controlled studies designed primarily to determine whether treatment of sleep disturbance independently improves gastrointestinal symptoms remain lacking [<citation rid="B38-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/jpepsy/jsad047" pmid="37515755" count="1">38</citation>,<citation rid="B42-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.2147/PHMT.S482343" pmcid="PMC11912920" pmid="40099110" count="1">42</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Therefore, sleep should currently be considered a clinically relevant and potentially modifiable treatment target within a broader biopsychosocial approach rather than an established stand-alone therapy for pediatric DGBIs. <sentence_start/>Indirect support comes from a randomized controlled trial in 60 young adults with IBS and comorbid insomnia, in which a four-week cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia intervention improved insomnia and reduced IBS symptom severity compared with the control condition [<citation rid="B56-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/ijerph192114174" pmid="36361052" pmcid="PMC9658882" count="1">56</citation>]. <sentence_start/>However, these findings cannot be directly extrapolated to pediatric patients. <sentence_start/>Future pediatric interventional studies should determine whether targeted treatment of sleep disturbance leads to clinically meaningful improvements in gastrointestinal symptoms, pain-related disability, and quality of life.
3. Stress and Its Impact on Gastrointestinal Symptoms
3.1. <sentence_start/>Stress Exposure and Neurobiological Stress Response

Acute and chronic stress are among the factors that may influence the course of pediatric DGBIs; however, their role should not be interpreted reductionistically as a purely ‘psychogenic’ cause of symptoms. <sentence_start/>Within the biopsychosocial model, stress is regarded as a modulator of the gut-brain axis, whereas symptom development results from interactions among biological predisposition, life experiences, emotional processes, family behaviors, the gut microbiota, gastrointestinal motility, and visceral hypersensitivity [<citation rid="B4-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1053/j.gastro.2016.02.032" pmid="27144617" count="1">4</citation>,<citation rid="B22-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.5409/wjcp.v14.i2.103323" pmid="40491742" pmcid="PMC11947882" count="1">22</citation>]. <sentence_start/>A review of anxiety disorders presenting gastrointestinal symptoms in children confirmed an association between anxiety and gastrointestinal symptoms while simultaneously emphasizing the difficulty in establishing a clear direction of causality [<citation rid="B49-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3345/cep.2024.01732" pmid="39810509" pmcid="PMC12062388" count="1">49</citation>].

Mechanistically, stress activates the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis and the autonomic nervous system. <sentence_start/>The release of cortisol and other stress mediators may affect intestinal motility, intestinal barrier permeability, immune responses, visceral neuronal excitability, and central pain processing [<citation rid="B22-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.5409/wjcp.v14.i2.103323" pmid="40491742" pmcid="PMC11947882" count="1">22</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Although direct assessment of neuroendocrine pathways is performed less frequently in pediatric populations than in adults, the available empirical evidence supports their important pathophysiological role. <sentence_start/>This is exemplified by the findings of a randomized trial evaluating the effects of a dance-yoga intervention on salivary cortisol concentrations in girls with FAP. <sentence_start/>These findings support the use of salivary cortisol as a non-invasive research biomarker of HPA-axis activity [<citation rid="B57-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fped.2022.836406" pmid="35633978" pmcid="PMC9133484" count="1">57</citation>]. <sentence_start/>However, salivary cortisol should not be interpreted as a validated clinical biomarker of stress severity or DGBI activity. <sentence_start/>Cortisol measurements are influenced by sampling time, collection procedures, covariate adjustment, and analytical methods, which limits comparability between studies [<citation rid="B58-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.bbih.2024.100936" pmid="39867845" pmcid="PMC11758133" count="1">58</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Data regarding autonomic function in children with FAP, IBS, and pain-predominant FGID further suggest that sympathovagal balance, vagal tone, and gastric motility may play important roles in modulating pain and dyspeptic symptoms [<citation rid="B52-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.jpain.2012.02.007" pmid="22520688" pmcid="PMC3566525" count="1">52</citation>,<citation rid="B53-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3748/wjg.v25.i1.95" pmid="30643361" pmcid="PMC6328964" count="1">53</citation>].
3.2. <sentence_start/>Psychiatric Comorbidity

Anxiety, depression, trauma, and somatization are particularly important considerations in the assessment of children with pain-predominant functional gastrointestinal disorders. <sentence_start/>Prospective studies by Shelby et al. demonstrated that children with functional abdominal pain are at increased risk of developing anxiety disorders during adolescence and young adulthood, even if abdominal pain resolves [<citation rid="B59-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1542/peds.2012-2191" pmid="23940244" pmcid="PMC3876748" count="1">59</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Walker et al. identified clinical subtypes of pediatric FAP that predicted subsequent FGID, chronic pain, and psychiatric comorbidity [<citation rid="B60-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.pain.2012.03.026" pmid="22721910" pmcid="PMC3413740" count="1">60</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Longitudinal studies provide further insight into factors associated with symptom persistence. <sentence_start/>Czyzewski et al. followed 76 children aged 7-10 years with functional abdominal pain for 18-24 months and found that baseline anxiety did not predict persistence of abdominal pain frequency. <sentence_start/>In contrast, symptom-related features consistent with IBS, particularly temporal relationships between abdominal pain and stooling documented in prospective pain and stool diaries and by parental report, were associated with persistence of pain at follow-up [<citation rid="B61-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1097/MPG.0000000000000947" pmid="26301615" pmcid="PMC4761339" count="1">61</citation>]. <sentence_start/>These findings suggest that gastrointestinal symptom phenotype may be more informative for pain persistence than anxiety alone in younger school-aged children.

Extraintestinal somatic symptoms may also identify children at increased risk of persistent DGBI-related morbidity. <sentence_start/>Dengler-Crish et al. prospectively followed children with functional abdominal pain for 4-15 years. <sentence_start/>Non-gastrointestinal somatic symptoms were assessed using the Children’s Somatization Inventory and included complaints such as dizziness, back pain, headaches, and sore muscles [<citation rid="B62-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1097/MPG.0b013e3181ec1d2e" pmid="21150653" pmcid="PMC3040560" count="1">62</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Among 188 participants with childhood functional abdominal pain, 35.6% met Rome III criteria for an FGID at follow-up, and baseline non-GI somatic symptom burden was significantly greater among those who subsequently met these criteria [<citation rid="B62-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1097/MPG.0b013e3181ec1d2e" pmid="21150653" pmcid="PMC3040560" count="1">62</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Clinically, the co-occurrence of abdominal pain with multiple extraintestinal somatic symptoms may therefore indicate a broader symptom burden and identify patients who warrant closer assessment of functional impairment and longitudinal symptom persistence; however, these observational findings do not establish causality.
3.3. <sentence_start/>Family and School Context

School-related stress may influence gastrointestinal symptoms through academic pressure, peer conflicts, school avoidance, limited access to toilet facilities, and anticipatory anxiety related to pain or defecation. <sentence_start/>A study conducted by Pollard et al. demonstrated a seasonal relationship between functional abdominal pain disorders (FAPDs) and anxiety levels that closely paralleled the school calendar. <sentence_start/>These findings suggest that school-related stressors may substantially modulate the clinical manifestation of symptoms in a subset of pediatric patients [<citation rid="B63-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1097/MPG.0000000000001886" pmid="29287016" pmcid="PMC6013328" count="1">63</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Data on school absenteeism further indicate that school avoidance and chronic symptoms may reinforce one another: pain leads to school absence, absenteeism increases anxiety about returning to school, and disruption of daily routines perpetuates functional impairment [<citation rid="B16-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fped.2024.1503783" pmid="39726527" pmcid="PMC11669597" count="1">16</citation>,<citation rid="B63-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1097/MPG.0000000000001886" pmid="29287016" pmcid="PMC6013328" count="1">63</citation>].

Family-related stress and parental responses are also clinically relevant. <sentence_start/>Overprotective responses to pain, frequent exemption of the child from routine responsibilities, reinforcement of illness behaviors, or parental catastrophizing may exacerbate functional disability, even when motivated by genuine concern. <sentence_start/>In this context, family education should avoid portraying symptoms as merely a “psychological problem”; instead, it should explain the biologically plausible gut-brain axis model and emphasize the importance of maintaining daily routines, physical activity, adequate sleep, regular meals, and a gradual return to school [<citation rid="B22-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.5409/wjcp.v14.i2.103323" pmid="40491742" pmcid="PMC11947882" count="1">22</citation>,<citation rid="B63-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1097/MPG.0000000000001886" pmid="29287016" pmcid="PMC6013328" count="1">63</citation>].
3.4. <sentence_start/>Modifiable Behavioral Patterns and Psychosocial Interventions

Stress also plays a significant role in functional constipation. <sentence_start/>A systematic review by Gozali et al. demonstrated that most pediatric studies reported an association between psychological stress and functional constipation, including school-related stress, family stress, and emotional factors [<citation rid="B48-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.11604/pamj.2023.46.8.41130" pmid="37928217" pmcid="PMC10620441" count="1">48</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The underlying mechanisms may include avoidance of defecation at school, embarrassment, toilet-related anxiety, painful bowel movements, increased pelvic floor muscle tension, and reinforcement of stool-withholding behaviors [<citation rid="B18-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1097/MPG.0000000000000266" pmid="24345831" count="1">18</citation>,<citation rid="B19-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3748/wjg.v29.i8.1261" pmid="36925458" pmcid="PMC10011959" count="1">19</citation>,<citation rid="B48-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.11604/pamj.2023.46.8.41130" pmid="37928217" pmcid="PMC10620441" count="1">48</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In IBS and functional dyspepsia, stress may exacerbate abdominal pain, diarrhea, constipation, nausea, postprandial fullness, and heartburn through its effects on gastrointestinal motility, visceral hypersensitivity, and interoceptive attention [<citation rid="B4-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1053/j.gastro.2016.02.032" pmid="27144617" count="1">4</citation>,<citation rid="B41-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1097/MD.0000000000025426" pmid="33787652" pmcid="PMC8021315" count="1">41</citation>,<citation rid="B53-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3748/wjg.v25.i1.95" pmid="30643361" pmcid="PMC6328964" count="1">53</citation>,<citation rid="B55-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1097/MPG.0b013e3181653a6f" pmid="18728527" pmcid="PMC3101499" count="1">55</citation>].

Evaluation of the available evidence indicates varying levels of certainty. <sentence_start/>The strongest evidence relates to the prevalence of FGID, their impact on quality of life, and the effectiveness of selected psychological interventions, as these areas are supported by systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and randomized controlled trials [<citation rid="B11-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/jcm10215087" pmid="34768604" pmcid="PMC8585107" count="1">11</citation>,<citation rid="B12-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1371/journal.pone.0126982" pmid="25992621" pmcid="PMC4439136" count="1">12</citation>,<citation rid="B44-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1001/jamapediatrics.2022.0313" pmid="35404394" pmcid="PMC9002716" count="1">44</citation>,<citation rid="B45-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/14651858.CD010971.pub2" pmid="28072460" pmcid="PMC6464036" count="1">45</citation>]. <sentence_start/>A meta-analysis of psychosocial interventions for FAP demonstrated that cognitive behavioral therapy and gut-directed hypnotherapy may reduce both the frequency and intensity of pain, although the quality of evidence varies across interventions and individual studies. <sentence_start/>More specifically, CBT was associated with greater treatment success compared with no intervention (RR 2.37, 95% CI 1.30-4.34, NNT = 5, moderate-certainty evidence), whereas the estimated benefit of hypnotherapy was also favorable but supported by lower-certainty evidence (RR 2.86, 95% CI 1.19-6.83, NNT = 5) [<citation rid="B44-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1001/jamapediatrics.2022.0313" pmid="35404394" pmcid="PMC9002716" count="1">44</citation>]. <sentence_start/>A Cochrane review of recurrent abdominal pain in children likewise supports the effectiveness of psychosocial interventions while emphasizing limitations related to small sample sizes, heterogeneous intervention protocols, and the risk of bias [<citation rid="B45-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/14651858.CD010971.pub2" pmid="28072460" pmcid="PMC6464036" count="1">45</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Randomized controlled trials evaluating gut-directed hypnotherapy and parent-involved cognitive behavioral therapy further strengthen the evidence that modulation of the stress response, parental behaviors, and coping strategies can reduce symptom severity in a subset of children [<citation rid="B46-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1001/jamapediatrics.2017.0091" pmid="28346581" count="1">46</citation>,<citation rid="B47-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/ajg.2010.106" pmid="20216531" pmcid="PMC2887246" count="1">47</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The above is illustrated in Figure 2.
4. Circadian Rhythm and Chronobiology of the Gastrointestinal Tract

The gastrointestinal (GI) tract is one of the major peripheral systems regulated by the circadian system. <sentence_start/>Circadian rhythms are endogenous biological oscillations with a period of approximately 24 h that coordinate physiological processes with environmental light-dark cycles. <sentence_start/>In mammals, the central circadian clock is located in the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) of the hypothalamus and is primarily entrained by light exposure, whereas peripheral clocks in the gastrointestinal tract are strongly influenced by feeding behavior, meal timing, and metabolic signals. <sentence_start/>Communication between the SCN and peripheral intestinal clocks contributes to the temporal coordination of digestion, nutrient absorption, immune responses, and host metabolism, thereby supporting gastrointestinal homeostasis [<citation rid="B25-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1210/endocr/bqaa167" pmid="32954405" pmcid="PMC7660274" count="1">25</citation>,<citation rid="B26-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41575-020-00401-5" pmid="33531700" count="1">26</citation>,<citation rid="B27-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1097/MCG.0000000000001333" pmid="32134798" pmcid="PMC7147411" count="1">27</citation>,<citation rid="B28-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1080/17474124.2019.1595588" pmid="30874451" pmcid="PMC6533073" count="1">28</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The mechanisms underlying these processes have been demonstrated predominantly in animal models and adult studies, while direct evidence in children and adolescents remains limited. <sentence_start/>This has been summarized in Table 2 and Table 3.

At the molecular level, circadian rhythms are generated through transcriptional-translational feedback loops involving core clock genes, including CLOCK, BMAL1 (ARNTL), PER1-3, and CRY1-2. <sentence_start/>These genes regulate the rhythmic expression of downstream targets involved in epithelial renewal, intestinal hormone secretion, barrier integrity, and inflammatory responses. <sentence_start/>Intestinal epithelial cells, enteric neurons, immune cells, and enteroendocrine cells possess autonomous circadian oscillators, allowing local regulation while remaining coordinated with the central circadian system [<citation rid="B25-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1210/endocr/bqaa167" pmid="32954405" pmcid="PMC7660274" count="1">25</citation>,<citation rid="B26-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41575-020-00401-5" pmid="33531700" count="1">26</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Evidence for these mechanisms is derived primarily from experimental and adult studies, and their specific relevance to pediatric disorders of gut-brain interaction (DGBI) remains incompletely established.

Circadian disruption caused by irregular sleep schedules, insufficient sleep duration, delayed sleep onset, night-time eating, or shift work has been associated with gastrointestinal and metabolic disturbances. <sentence_start/>Among adolescents, one common manifestation of circadian misalignment is social jetlag, defined as the discrepancy between biological and socially imposed sleep schedules, typically resulting from delayed sleep during weekends followed by earlier awakening on school days. <sentence_start/>Pediatric and adolescent research has primarily investigated associations between social jetlag, sleep disturbances, dietary behavior, obesity, and metabolic health, whereas direct evidence concerning gastrointestinal symptoms or disorders of gut-brain interaction (DGBI) remains very limited. <sentence_start/>Thus, the potential relationship between social jetlag and pediatric DGBI is currently supported mainly by indirect evidence and biological plausibility rather than by direct pediatric studies [<citation rid="B25-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1210/endocr/bqaa167" pmid="32954405" pmcid="PMC7660274" count="1">25</citation>,<citation rid="B29-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1155/2022/2939921" pmid="35320972" pmcid="PMC8938076" count="1">29</citation>].
4.1. <sentence_start/>Circadian Regulation of Gastrointestinal Motility and Secretion

Virtually every component of gastrointestinal physiology exhibits some degree of circadian rhythmicity. <sentence_start/>Gastric emptying, intestinal motility, digestive enzyme secretion, bile acid metabolism, and gastrointestinal hormone release demonstrate temporal variation across the day [<citation rid="B25-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1210/endocr/bqaa167" pmid="32954405" pmcid="PMC7660274" count="1">25</citation>,<citation rid="B26-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41575-020-00401-5" pmid="33531700" count="1">26</citation>,<citation rid="B27-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1097/MCG.0000000000001333" pmid="32134798" pmcid="PMC7147411" count="1">27</citation>,<citation rid="B28-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1080/17474124.2019.1595588" pmid="30874451" pmcid="PMC6533073" count="1">28</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Experimental and adult studies suggest that gastrointestinal motility and digestive secretions are generally enhanced during the active or feeding phase and reduced during the resting phase. <sentence_start/>Disruption of these rhythms may contribute to alterations in gastrointestinal motility and symptoms such as constipation, diarrhea, and abdominal discomfort [<citation rid="B26-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41575-020-00401-5" pmid="33531700" count="1">26</citation>,<citation rid="B27-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1097/MCG.0000000000001333" pmid="32134798" pmcid="PMC7147411" count="1">27</citation>,<citation rid="B28-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1080/17474124.2019.1595588" pmid="30874451" pmcid="PMC6533073" count="1">28</citation>]. <sentence_start/>However, direct evidence linking circadian disruption with gastrointestinal motility disorders or DGBI in children is currently limited.

Enteroendocrine hormones, including glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1), glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide (GIP), peptide YY (PYY), ghrelin, and serotonin, demonstrate diurnal variation and contribute to the coordination of appetite regulation, gastrointestinal motility, visceral signaling, and metabolic homeostasis with feeding cycles [<citation rid="B25-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1210/endocr/bqaa167" pmid="32954405" pmcid="PMC7660274" count="1">25</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Experimental and adult studies suggest that alterations in enteroendocrine signaling may influence gastric emptying, intestinal transit, appetite, and visceral sensitivity, which are relevant to symptom domains commonly observed in DGBI, including abdominal pain, bloating, altered bowel habits, and meal-related gastrointestinal symptoms. <sentence_start/>In particular, altered signaling involving GLP-1, PYY, and ghrelin may affect gastrointestinal motility and appetite, while serotonin plays an important role in enteric signaling and intestinal motility [<citation rid="B25-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1210/endocr/bqaa167" pmid="32954405" pmcid="PMC7660274" count="1">25</citation>,<citation rid="B26-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41575-020-00401-5" pmid="33531700" count="1">26</citation>]. <sentence_start/>However, these associations are supported predominantly by experimental and adult data, and direct evidence linking circadian alterations in enteroendocrine hormones to specific pediatric DGBI subtypes remains limited.

The evidence summarized in this subsection is derived predominantly from animal and adult studies. <sentence_start/>Direct pediatric evidence regarding circadian regulation of gastrointestinal motility, secretion, and enteroendocrine signaling in DGBI is scarce.
4.2. <sentence_start/>Circadian Rhythm and Intestinal Barrier Integrity

Maintenance of the intestinal epithelial barrier is another process influenced by circadian regulation. <sentence_start/>Tight junction proteins, epithelial regeneration, mucus secretion, antimicrobial peptide production, and intestinal immune activity display daily oscillations associated with local clock gene activity [<citation rid="B26-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41575-020-00401-5" pmid="33531700" count="1">26</citation>,<citation rid="B29-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1155/2022/2939921" pmid="35320972" pmcid="PMC8938076" count="1">29</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Experimental studies, particularly in animal models, indicate that disruption of circadian rhythms may alter the expression and organization of tight junction proteins, including occludin and claudins, and increase intestinal permeability [<citation rid="B26-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41575-020-00401-5" pmid="33531700" count="1">26</citation>,<citation rid="B29-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1155/2022/2939921" pmid="35320972" pmcid="PMC8938076" count="1">29</citation>].

Increased intestinal permeability has been proposed as one of several potential mechanisms contributing to gastrointestinal symptoms in selected functional gastrointestinal disorders; however, it should not be considered an established or universal mechanism across all pediatric DGBI subtypes. <sentence_start/>The relevance of altered barrier function may differ according to the specific disorder, symptom profile, and individual biological context. <sentence_start/>Animal studies further suggest that dysregulation of core clock genes may affect epithelial barrier function and inflammatory responses, while human evidence remains more limited and is derived predominantly from adult populations [<citation rid="B29-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1155/2022/2939921" pmid="35320972" pmcid="PMC8938076" count="1">29</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Thus, circadian effects on intestinal barrier integrity should currently be regarded as a potential mechanistic pathway rather than a general explanation for pediatric DGBI.

Evidence concerning circadian regulation of intestinal barrier integrity is derived predominantly from animal models and adult studies. <sentence_start/>Direct pediatric evidence, particularly in children with DGBI, remains insufficient.
4.3. <sentence_start/>Gut Microbiota and Feeding Rhythms

Accumulating evidence indicates that the gut microbiota exhibits circadian fluctuations in both microbial composition and metabolic activity. <sentence_start/>These rhythmic changes appear to be strongly influenced by feeding patterns and meal timing rather than by light exposure alone. <sentence_start/>Microbial metabolites, including short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs), may also display diurnal variation and influence intestinal immunity, epithelial metabolism, and peripheral clock gene expression [<citation rid="B26-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41575-020-00401-5" pmid="33531700" count="1">26</citation>,<citation rid="B30-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.5114/pg.2023.132437" pmcid="PMC10985757" pmid="38571538" count="1">30</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Most evidence supporting these mechanisms comes from animal and adult studies.

Interpretation of microbiome findings in children requires particular caution because gut microbial composition and rhythmicity are influenced by several age-dependent and methodological factors. <sentence_start/>Sampling time is especially relevant because microbial abundance and metabolite production may vary across the day. <sentence_start/>In addition, recent or ongoing antibiotic exposure can substantially alter microbial composition and diversity. <sentence_start/>Age and pubertal stage are also important determinants of the developing gut microbiome, while dietary composition, meal timing, and overall nutritional patterns may independently influence microbial diversity and metabolic activity. <sentence_start/>These factors may therefore confound associations between sleep or circadian disruption and microbiome characteristics in pediatric populations.

Conversely, experimental studies indicate that irregular eating patterns, nocturnal food intake, and circadian misalignment may disrupt microbial rhythmicity and alter microbial metabolites. <sentence_start/>Such changes have been associated with metabolic dysfunction, obesity, low-grade inflammation, and gastrointestinal abnormalities [<citation rid="B26-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41575-020-00401-5" pmid="33531700" count="1">26</citation>,<citation rid="B30-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.5114/pg.2023.132437" pmcid="PMC10985757" pmid="38571538" count="1">30</citation>]. <sentence_start/>A bidirectional relationship has also been proposed, whereby host circadian rhythms influence the microbiota while microbial metabolites and immune signaling may contribute to the synchronization of peripheral clocks. <sentence_start/>However, the clinical significance of these mechanisms in pediatric DGBI remains unclear.

Pediatric evidence is emerging but remains limited. <sentence_start/>Available studies in children and adolescents have primarily examined associations between sleep disturbances, circadian characteristics, metabolic health, and gut microbiota composition rather than gastrointestinal symptoms or DGBI. <sentence_start/>A recent systematic review of children with obstructive sleep apnea syndrome identified alterations in gut microbiota composition, supporting a possible relationship between sleep-related disturbances and the intestinal microbiome [<citation rid="B31-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.sleep.2024.06.002" pmid="38878352" count="1">31</citation>]. <sentence_start/>However, these findings cannot be directly interpreted as evidence that circadian disruption causes DGBI or gastrointestinal dysfunction in children. <sentence_start/>The heterogeneity of pediatric populations and potential confounding by age, pubertal development, diet, medication exposure, and sampling conditions further limits direct comparison between studies.

Evidence note: Evidence for microbiota-circadian interactions is largely derived from animal and adult studies, with emerging pediatric evidence. <sentence_start/>Direct studies investigating the relationship between circadian disruption, gut microbiota, and pediatric DGBI remain limited [<citation rid="B26-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41575-020-00401-5" pmid="33531700" count="1">26</citation>,<citation rid="B30-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.5114/pg.2023.132437" pmcid="PMC10985757" pmid="38571538" count="1">30</citation>,<citation rid="B31-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.sleep.2024.06.002" pmid="38878352" count="1">31</citation>].

Compared with adult populations, evidence regarding gastrointestinal chronobiology in children and adolescents remains relatively limited. <sentence_start/>Most pediatric studies have focused on sleep duration, circadian preference, dietary behavior, obesity, metabolic health, or gut microbiota rather than direct gastrointestinal outcomes. <sentence_start/>Consequently, the potential role of circadian disruption in pediatric DGBI is currently supported mainly by biological plausibility and extrapolation from adult and experimental research.

Studies specifically evaluating social jetlag and gastrointestinal physiology in children are scarce, and direct evidence linking circadian disruption with intestinal permeability, gastrointestinal motility, or DGBI in pediatric populations remains insufficient. <sentence_start/>Therefore, regular sleep-wake schedules and consistent meal timing may represent plausible strategies for supporting gastrointestinal and metabolic health, but evidence demonstrating that these measures prevent or improve pediatric DGBI is currently lacking. <sentence_start/>Further longitudinal and interventional studies in pediatric populations are required to determine whether circadian regulation represents a clinically relevant modifiable factor in the development and management of DGBI [<citation rid="B25-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1210/endocr/bqaa167" pmid="32954405" pmcid="PMC7660274" count="1">25</citation>,<citation rid="B26-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41575-020-00401-5" pmid="33531700" count="1">26</citation>,<citation rid="B27-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1097/MCG.0000000000001333" pmid="32134798" pmcid="PMC7147411" count="1">27</citation>,<citation rid="B28-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1080/17474124.2019.1595588" pmid="30874451" pmcid="PMC6533073" count="1">28</citation>,<citation rid="B29-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1155/2022/2939921" pmid="35320972" pmcid="PMC8938076" count="1">29</citation>,<citation rid="B30-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.5114/pg.2023.132437" pmcid="PMC10985757" pmid="38571538" count="1">30</citation>,<citation rid="B31-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.sleep.2024.06.002" pmid="38878352" count="1">31</citation>].
5. <sentence_start/>Diet and Eating Habits

Diet is one of the important modifiable factors that may influence symptoms of disorders of gut-brain interaction (DGBIs). <sentence_start/>Beyond providing nutrients, dietary patterns may affect gastrointestinal motility, microbial composition, fermentation processes, intestinal permeability, and gut-brain signaling, potentially contributing to abdominal pain, bloating, and altered bowel habits [<citation rid="B32-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/nu15122708" pmid="37375612" pmcid="PMC10302595" count="1">32</citation>,<citation rid="B33-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1080/17474124.2022.2055547" pmid="35311425" count="1">33</citation>,<citation rid="B34-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s11938-023-00433-1" count="1">34</citation>]. <sentence_start/>However, evidence derived from general metabolic, microbiome, or adult gastrointestinal research should be distinguished from direct evidence in children with DGBIs.

Western dietary patterns characterized by a high intake of ultra-processed foods, refined carbohydrates, saturated fats, and sugar-sweetened beverages have been associated with poorer gastrointestinal and metabolic health and with alterations in gut microbial composition. <sentence_start/>In contrast, dietary patterns rich in fruits, vegetables, legumes, and whole grains, including Mediterranean-style diets, may support overall metabolic and gastrointestinal health through increased intake of fiber and bioactive compounds and potential effects on the gut microbiome [<citation rid="B33-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1080/17474124.2022.2055547" pmid="35311425" count="1">33</citation>]. <sentence_start/>However, direct evidence demonstrating that specific dietary patterns prevent or improve pediatric DGBIs remains limited, and associations observed in adult or general-population studies should not be interpreted as established causal relationships in children.

Meal timing may also influence gastrointestinal function. <sentence_start/>Irregular eating patterns, prolonged fasting, and breakfast skipping may affect gastrointestinal motility, circadian regulation of digestive processes, and overall dietary quality. <sentence_start/>Although direct pediatric evidence linking meal timing with DGBI symptoms is limited, regular meal consumption is commonly included in the dietary management of pediatric DGBIs [<citation rid="B33-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1080/17474124.2022.2055547" pmid="35311425" count="1">33</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Thus, regular meal patterns may represent a reasonable low-risk component of symptom management, while the magnitude of their specific therapeutic effect in children remains uncertain.

Dietary fiber plays an important role in maintaining gastrointestinal health, but its effects depend on the amount, type, and individual tolerance. <sentence_start/>Adequate dietary fiber intake as part of a balanced, age-appropriate diet is generally recommended in children. <sentence_start/>This should be distinguished from therapeutic fiber supplementation, which may be considered in selected patients with specific symptoms or disorders. <sentence_start/>Soluble, gel-forming fibers such as psyllium may improve stool consistency and bowel function and have been studied in functional constipation and functional abdominal pain disorders [<citation rid="B23-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/nu10111650" pmid="30400292" pmcid="PMC6267171" count="1">23</citation>,<citation rid="B32-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/nu15122708" pmid="37375612" pmcid="PMC10302595" count="1">32</citation>,<citation rid="B33-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1080/17474124.2022.2055547" pmid="35311425" count="1">33</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In contrast, some poorly tolerated or excessive amounts of insoluble or highly fermentable fiber may increase gas production, bloating, or abdominal discomfort in susceptible individuals. <sentence_start/>Therefore, fiber intake should be individualized according to age, baseline dietary intake, predominant symptoms, and tolerance rather than increased indiscriminately.

Among dietary interventions, the low-fermentable oligosaccharides, disaccharides, monosaccharides, and polyols (low-FODMAP) diet has received considerable attention. <sentence_start/>FODMAPs are poorly absorbed carbohydrates that increase luminal water content and undergo bacterial fermentation, potentially leading to gas production, intestinal distension, and gastrointestinal symptoms. <sentence_start/>Although the low-FODMAP diet has demonstrated efficacy in adults with irritable bowel syndrome, evidence in children remains limited and heterogeneous. <sentence_start/>Available pediatric trials include relatively small sample sizes and provide low-certainty evidence [<citation rid="B24-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/nmo.14392" pmid="35535019" pmcid="PMC9529764" count="1">24</citation>,<citation rid="B32-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/nu15122708" pmid="37375612" pmcid="PMC10302595" count="1">32</citation>,<citation rid="B33-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1080/17474124.2022.2055547" pmid="35311425" count="1">33</citation>,<citation rid="B35-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/nu15102295" pmid="37242178" pmcid="PMC10223978" count="1">35</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Therefore, routine implementation of a strict low-FODMAP diet is not recommended in children. <sentence_start/>In selected patients with persistent symptoms, it may be considered under the supervision of an experienced pediatric dietitian, with an appropriately structured elimination and reintroduction phase to minimize nutritional risks [<citation rid="B32-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/nu15122708" pmid="37375612" pmcid="PMC10302595" count="1">32</citation>,<citation rid="B33-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1080/17474124.2022.2055547" pmid="35311425" count="1">33</citation>,<citation rid="B35-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/nu15102295" pmid="37242178" pmcid="PMC10223978" count="1">35</citation>].

Before initiating restrictive or elimination diets, an appropriate clinical assessment should be performed to exclude relevant organic diseases when indicated by the clinical presentation. <sentence_start/>This may include evaluation for conditions such as celiac disease, particularly when symptoms, growth abnormalities, anemia, family history, or other clinical features raise suspicion. <sentence_start/>Elimination of gluten should therefore not be initiated before appropriate assessment for celiac disease when clinically indicated, as dietary gluten restriction may interfere with subsequent diagnostic testing.

It is also important to distinguish food intolerance or hypersensitivity from food allergy. <sentence_start/>In children with DGBIs, symptoms attributed to specific foods may be related to carbohydrate malabsorption, intestinal fermentation, altered gastrointestinal motility, or visceral hypersensitivity rather than IgE-mediated food allergy [<citation rid="B32-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/nu15122708" pmid="37375612" pmcid="PMC10302595" count="1">32</citation>,<citation rid="B33-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1080/17474124.2022.2055547" pmid="35311425" count="1">33</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Consequently, routine elimination of gluten, lactose, or other foods without an appropriate clinical indication is not supported by current evidence.

Restrictive diets require particular caution in pediatric populations because they may lead to inadequate intake of energy, calcium, vitamin D, iron, zinc, and dietary fiber and may increase the risk of disordered eating and impaired growth. <sentence_start/>Therefore, current approaches emphasize individualized dietary counseling rather than empiric food exclusion. <sentence_start/>Initial management should focus on establishing regular meal patterns, maintaining adequate hydration, ensuring age-appropriate dietary fiber intake, and reducing excessive consumption of ultra-processed foods and sugar-sweetened beverages before considering more restrictive dietary interventions [<citation rid="B32-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/nu15122708" pmid="37375612" pmcid="PMC10302595" count="1">32</citation>,<citation rid="B33-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1080/17474124.2022.2055547" pmid="35311425" count="1">33</citation>,<citation rid="B35-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/nu15102295" pmid="37242178" pmcid="PMC10223978" count="1">35</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The above has been summarized in Table 4.
6. <sentence_start/>Reciprocal Interactions Between Sleep, Stress, Circadian Rhythm, and Diet: An Integrative Model

Sleep, stress, circadian rhythm, and diet are closely interconnected components of the gut-brain axis. <sentence_start/>Rather than acting as isolated factors, they may influence gastrointestinal function through overlapping neuroendocrine, autonomic, immune, metabolic, and microbial pathways, thereby contributing to the persistence and severity of disorders of gut-brain interaction (DGBIs) [<citation rid="B34-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s11938-023-00433-1" count="1">34</citation>,<citation rid="B36-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fendo.2023.1130689" pmcid="PMC10316519" pmid="37404311" count="1">36</citation>,<citation rid="B37-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/nu15122743" pmid="37375647" pmcid="PMC10303702" count="1">37</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The main interactions are summarized in Table 2.

Among these factors, the relationship between psychological stress and sleep is relatively well established. <sentence_start/>Psychological stress activates the hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal (HPA) axis and the sympathetic nervous system, while chronic stress may impair sleep quality and promote sleep fragmentation. <sentence_start/>Conversely, insufficient or disrupted sleep can increase stress reactivity and HPA-axis activity, potentially creating a reinforcing cycle [<citation rid="B34-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s11938-023-00433-1" count="1">34</citation>,<citation rid="B36-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fendo.2023.1130689" pmcid="PMC10316519" pmid="37404311" count="1">36</citation>]. <sentence_start/>These alterations may affect gastrointestinal motility, visceral sensitivity, intestinal immune signaling, and barrier function, which may contribute to gastrointestinal symptoms in susceptible individuals [<citation rid="B34-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s11938-023-00433-1" count="1">34</citation>,<citation rid="B36-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fendo.2023.1130689" pmcid="PMC10316519" pmid="37404311" count="1">36</citation>].

Circadian timing provides an additional layer of interaction. <sentence_start/>Irregular sleep-wake schedules and social jetlag may be accompanied by delayed or irregular meal timing, breakfast skipping, and less favorable dietary choices [<citation rid="B25-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1210/endocr/bqaa167" pmid="32954405" pmcid="PMC7660274" count="1">25</citation>,<citation rid="B26-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41575-020-00401-5" pmid="33531700" count="1">26</citation>,<citation rid="B27-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1097/MCG.0000000000001333" pmid="32134798" pmcid="PMC7147411" count="1">27</citation>,<citation rid="B28-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1080/17474124.2019.1595588" pmid="30874451" pmcid="PMC6533073" count="1">28</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Conversely, late or irregular food intake may influence peripheral circadian rhythms in the gastrointestinal tract and metabolic tissues. <sentence_start/>Although these relationships are biologically plausible and supported by experimental and adult data, the extent to which circadian misalignment directly contributes to pediatric DGBIs remains insufficiently established [<citation rid="B25-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1210/endocr/bqaa167" pmid="32954405" pmcid="PMC7660274" count="1">25</citation>,<citation rid="B26-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/s41575-020-00401-5" pmid="33531700" count="1">26</citation>,<citation rid="B27-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1097/MCG.0000000000001333" pmid="32134798" pmcid="PMC7147411" count="1">27</citation>,<citation rid="B28-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1080/17474124.2019.1595588" pmid="30874451" pmcid="PMC6533073" count="1">28</citation>,<citation rid="B37-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/nu15122743" pmid="37375647" pmcid="PMC10303702" count="1">37</citation>].

Diet and sleep may likewise influence each other. <sentence_start/>Dietary composition and meal timing have been associated with sleep duration and quality, while inadequate sleep may alter appetite regulation and food preferences, potentially favoring energy-dense foods [<citation rid="B37-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/nu15122743" pmid="37375647" pmcid="PMC10303702" count="1">37</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Dietary patterns characterized by greater intake of fiber and plant-based foods may additionally support microbial metabolism and short-chain fatty acid (SCFA) production, whereas highly processed dietary patterns may have opposite effects. <sentence_start/>However, the clinical relevance of these pathways for individual pediatric DGBI subtypes remains incompletely defined [<citation rid="B37-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/nu15122743" pmid="37375647" pmcid="PMC10303702" count="1">37</citation>].

The gut microbiota may represent one of the pathways through which these factors converge. <sentence_start/>Sleep disruption, psychological stress, circadian misalignment, and dietary changes have each been associated with alterations in microbial composition or function, while microbiota-derived metabolites may participate in immune, metabolic, and gut-brain signaling [<citation doi="10.3390/nu15122743" pmid="37375647" pmcid="PMC10303702" count="1">37</citation>,<citation rid="B38-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/jpepsy/jsad047" pmid="37515755"
