rid="B67-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/14651858.CD012849.pub2" pmid="36799531" pmcid="PMC9945052" count="1">67</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Therefore, a direct causal pathway linking lifestyle-related disruption to microbiome changes and subsequently to DGBI symptoms should not yet be assumed.

Taken together, the available evidence supports a reciprocal model in which sleep, psychological stress, circadian timing, and dietary behavior may reinforce one another and interact with gut-brain signaling. <sentence_start/>However, the strength of evidence differs across individual pathways. <sentence_start/>The bidirectional relationships between stress and sleep and the influence of diet and meal timing on circadian physiology are relatively well supported, whereas microbiome-mediated pathways and their specific contribution to pediatric DGBIs remain largely mechanistic or indirect. <sentence_start/>Consequently, clinical management may benefit from considering these factors together rather than in isolation, although further pediatric intervention studies are needed to determine whether multicomponent lifestyle interventions provide greater benefits than single-component approaches [<citation rid="B25-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1210/endocr/bqaa167" pmid="32954405" pmcid="PMC7660274" count="1">25</citation>,<citation rid="B38-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/jpepsy/jsad047" pmid="37515755" count="1">38</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The main model is presented in Table 5.
7. Clinical Implications and Current Limitations

The management of pediatric disorders of gut-brain interaction (DGBIs) should adopt a biopsychosocial approach, integrating gastrointestinal symptoms with lifestyle, psychological, developmental, and environmental factors. <sentence_start/>The clinical evaluation of a child with suspected DGBI should proceed in a stepwise and age-appropriate manner rather than being framed as a choice between no investigation and an extensive diagnostic work-up. <sentence_start/>Before assigning a positive DGBI diagnosis, clinicians should characterize symptom onset, duration and severity, growth trajectory, stool and vomiting patterns, relationships of symptoms to eating and defecation, dietary and medication exposures, psychosocial context and relevant family history, followed by a focused physical examination [<citation rid="B5-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1053/j.gastro.2016.02.015" pmid="27144632" count="1">5</citation>,<citation rid="B17-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fped.2025.1576698" pmid="40433476" pmcid="PMC12108103" count="1">17</citation>,<citation rid="B68-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1080/17474124.2017.1282820" pmid="28092724" count="1">68</citation>,<citation rid="B69-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/nrgastro.2015.21" pmid="25666642" count="1">69</citation>,<citation rid="B70-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.2147/PHMT.S287719" pmcid="PMC8354769" pmid="34393542" count="1">70</citation>]. <sentence_start/>The threshold, urgency, and extent of further investigations depend on the child’s age, clinical phenotype, symptom severity, growth, and the presence of alarm features.

Alarm features that should prompt consideration of targeted investigation include involuntary weight loss or deceleration of growth, delayed puberty, gastrointestinal bleeding, excessive or persistent vomiting, severe chronic diarrhoea, persistent right upper- or right lower-quadrant pain, perianal disease, dysphagia, unexplained fever or arthritis and a family history of inflammatory bowel disease or celiac disease [<citation rid="B5-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1053/j.gastro.2016.02.015" pmid="27144632" count="1">5</citation>,<citation rid="B17-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fped.2025.1576698" pmid="40433476" pmcid="PMC12108103" count="1">17</citation>,<citation rid="B68-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1080/17474124.2017.1282820" pmid="28092724" count="1">68</citation>,<citation rid="B69-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/nrgastro.2015.21" pmid="25666642" count="1">69</citation>,<citation rid="B70-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.2147/PHMT.S287719" pmcid="PMC8354769" pmid="34393542" count="1">70</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Depending on the clinical presentation, targeted investigations may include complete blood count, inflammatory markers, faecal calprotectin or lactoferrin, celiac serology, liver or pancreatic tests, urinalysis, imaging, or endoscopy [<citation rid="B70-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.2147/PHMT.S287719" pmcid="PMC8354769" pmid="34393542" count="1">70</citation>]. <sentence_start/>In the absence of alarm features and when the symptom pattern is compatible with current DGBI diagnostic criteria, routine extensive testing is generally of low yield; however, limited investigations may still be appropriate depending on age, symptom phenotype, and diagnostic uncertainty [<citation rid="B17-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fped.2025.1576698" pmid="40433476" pmcid="PMC12108103" count="1">17</citation>,<citation rid="B68-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1080/17474124.2017.1282820" pmid="28092724" count="1">68</citation>,<citation rid="B69-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/nrgastro.2015.21" pmid="25666642" count="1">69</citation>,<citation rid="B70-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.2147/PHMT.S287719" pmcid="PMC8354769" pmid="34393542" count="1">70</citation>].

First-line management should emphasize non-pharmacological interventions. <sentence_start/>Families should be encouraged to establish regular sleep schedules, maintain consistent meal timing, consume a balanced diet with adequate fiber and fluid intake, increase daily physical activity, and limit evening caffeine consumption and screen exposure. <sentence_start/>These low-risk interventions may improve gastrointestinal symptoms while also benefiting mental and metabolic health [<citation rid="B17-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fped.2025.1576698" pmid="40433476" pmcid="PMC12108103" count="1">17</citation>,<citation rid="B18-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1097/MPG.0000000000000266" pmid="24345831" count="1">18</citation>,<citation Physical activity and screen exposure should be considered secondary supportive lifestyle domains in the present review because direct evidence linking them independently to pediatric DGBI outcomes is substantially more limited than the evidence available for sleep, stress, and dietary factors. <sentence_start/>In a small cross-sectional study of adolescents with functional abdominal pain, total daily screen time did not correlate with the severity of abdominal pain or other gastrointestinal symptoms [<citation rid="B71-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fped.2020.592972" pmid="33330286" pmcid="PMC7732463" count="1">71</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Conversely, an accelerometer-based study of preschool children suggested an association between higher moderate-to-vigorous physical activity and more favorable defecation habits [<citation rid="B72-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/children10060951" pmid="37371183" pmcid="PMC10297704" count="1">72</citation>]. <sentence_start/>However, this study did not evaluate Rome-defined DGBIs and cannot establish causality. <sentence_start/>Consequently, recommendations regarding physical activity and screen exposure should primarily be framed as components of general health, maintenance of daily routines, and sleep hygiene rather than as established DGBI-specific treatments.

Referral to additional specialists should be considered when symptoms persist despite initial management or when specific problems are identified. <sentence_start/>Children with suspected nutritional deficiencies, restrictive eating patterns, or those requiring dietary interventions such as a low-FODMAP diet should be referred to a registered pediatric dietitian. <sentence_start/>Patients with significant anxiety, depression, chronic stress, or maladaptive coping strategies may benefit from evaluation by a psychologist, particularly for cognitive behavioral therapy or gut-directed hypnotherapy. <sentence_start/>Referral to a pediatric gastroenterologist is indicated in the presence of alarm features, diagnostic uncertainty, treatment failure, or suspected organic gastrointestinal disease [<citation rid="B17-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fped.2025.1576698" pmid="40433476" pmcid="PMC12108103" count="1">17</citation>,<citation Overall, current evidence supports a multidisciplinary, patient-centered approach that targets modifiable lifestyle factors alongside symptom management rather than focusing exclusively on gastrointestinal manifestations.
Limitations of Current Evidence

Despite increasing recognition of the role of lifestyle factors, including diet, sleep, stress, and circadian regulation, in pediatric disorders of gut-brain interaction (DGBIs), several limitations affect the interpretation of current evidence. <sentence_start/>Most available studies are observational, making it difficult to establish causal relationships between lifestyle exposures and gastrointestinal symptoms. <sentence_start/>Associations between poor sleep, psychological stress, dietary patterns, and DGBIs may reflect bidirectional interactions, where symptoms themselves contribute to sleep disruption, altered eating behavior, and increased psychological burden [<citation rid="B32-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/nu15122708" pmid="37375612" pmcid="PMC10302595" count="1">32</citation>,<citation rid="B33-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1080/17474124.2022.2055547" pmid="35311425" count="1">33</citation>,<citation rid="B38-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/jpepsy/jsad047" pmid="37515755" count="1">38</citation>,<citation rid="B42-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.2147/PHMT.S482343" pmcid="PMC11912920" pmid="40099110" count="1">42</citation>,<citation rid="B44-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1001/jamapediatrics.2022.0313" pmid="35404394" pmcid="PMC9002716" count="1">44</citation>,<citation rid="B45-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/14651858.CD010971.pub2" pmid="28072460" pmcid="PMC6464036" count="1">45</citation>,<citation rid="B69-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/nrgastro.2015.21" pmid="25666642" count="1">69</citation>].

Another important limitation is the heterogeneity of diagnostic criteria and assessment methods. <sentence_start/>Studies have used different definitions of functional gastrointestinal disorders, including Rome III and Rome IV criteria, which complicate comparisons between populations. <sentence_start/>Similarly, evaluation of sleep quality, stress levels, dietary intake, and physical activity is frequently based on self-reported questionnaires, parental reports, or heterogeneous measurement tools, limiting the accuracy and reproducibility of findings [<citation rid="B11-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/jcm10215087" pmid="34768604" pmcid="PMC8585107" count="1">11</citation>,<citation rid="B14-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1177/2333794X211022265" pmcid="PMC8170292" pmid="34104704" count="1">14</citation>,<citation rid="B32-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/nu15122708" pmid="37375612" pmcid="PMC10302595" count="1">32</citation>,<citation rid="B33-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1080/17474124.2022.2055547" pmid="35311425" count="1">33</citation>,<citation rid="B38-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/jpepsy/jsad047" pmid="37515755" count="1">38</citation>,<citation rid="B42-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.2147/PHMT.S482343" pmcid="PMC11912920" pmid="40099110" count="1">42</citation>,<citation rid="B68-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1080/17474124.2017.1282820" pmid="28092724" count="1">68</citation>,<citation rid="B69-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/nrgastro.2015.21" pmid="25666642" count="1">69</citation>].

Additional sources of heterogeneity and confounding should also be considered. <sentence_start/>Pediatric cohorts often span broad age ranges, and while developmental and pubertal stage may influence sleep patterns, circadian timing, psychological responses, and symptom reporting, these variables are not consistently stratified or adjusted for across studies [<citation rid="B11-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/jcm10215087" pmid="34768604" pmcid="PMC8585107" count="1">11</citation>,<citation rid="B38-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/jpepsy/jsad047" pmid="37515755" rid="B43-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1111/nmo.14992" pmid="39737536" pmcid="PMC11996607" count="1">43</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Psychiatric comorbidity represents another major potential confounder because anxiety, depression, and somatic symptoms are associated with both DGBI severity and sleep- or stress-related outcomes [<citation rid="B38-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/jpepsy/jsad047" pmid="37515755" count="1">38</citation>,<citation rid="B49-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3345/cep.2024.01732" pmid="39810509" rid="B60-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1016/j.pain.2012.03.026" pmid="22721910" pmcid="PMC3413740" count="1">60</citation>,<citation rid="B61-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1097/MPG.0000000000000947" pmid="26301615" pmcid="PMC4761339" count="1">61</citation>,<citation rid="B62-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1097/MPG.0b013e3181ec1d2e" pmid="21150653" pmcid="PMC3040560" count="1">62</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Consequently, associations attributed to an individual lifestyle factor may partly reflect shared psychological or developmental determinants.

Microbiome-related studies are additionally vulnerable to confounding by antibiotic and probiotic exposure. <sentence_start/>A recent systematic review of 89 studies involving 9712 children found that systemic antibiotic exposure was consistently associated with alterations in gut microbial composition and reduced alpha diversity, with some effects persisting for months after treatment [<citation rid="B73-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/falgy.2024.1458688" pmid="39435363" pmcid="PMC11491438" count="1">73</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Probiotic interventions are likewise highly heterogeneous with respect to strain, dose, treatment duration, and outcome assessment [<citation rid="B67-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/14651858.CD012849.pub2" pmid="36799531" pmcid="PMC9945052" count="1">67</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Failure to adequately record or adjust for these exposures may therefore contribute to inconsistent microbiome findings across pediatric DGBI studies.

Socioeconomic and cultural context may further limit generalizability. <sentence_start/>Earlier pediatric meta-analytic data demonstrated substantial geographic variability and inconsistent associations between socioeconomic status and functional abdominal pain [<citation rid="B12-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1371/journal.pone.0126982" pmid="25992621" pmcid="PMC4439136" count="1">12</citation>]. <sentence_start/>More recent global evidence confirms marked between-study heterogeneity: a meta-analysis of 67 studies involving 1,712,737 children and adolescents from 34 countries estimated an overall FAPD prevalence of 10.89% (95% CI 9.51-12.48%), with very high heterogeneity (<italic>I</italic><sup>2</sup> = 95.90%) [<citation rid="B74-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.5009/gnl250225" pmid="40852741" pmcid="PMC13180508" count="1">74</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Such variation may reflect differences in diagnostic criteria, sampling, symptom reporting, healthcare access, socioeconomic conditions, and cultural context and should caution against assuming uniform associations across populations. <sentence_start/>Publication bias and selective-reporting bias should also be considered, particularly in areas dominated by small observational studies or intervention trials [<citation rid="B32-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/nu15122708" pmid="37375612" pmcid="PMC10302595" count="1">32</citation>,<citation rid="B33-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1080/17474124.2022.2055547" pmid="35311425" count="1">33</citation>,<citation rid="B38-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/jpepsy/jsad047" pmid="37515755" count="1">38</citation>,<citation rid="B44-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1001/jamapediatrics.2022.0313" pmid="35404394" pmcid="PMC9002716" count="1">44</citation>,<citation rid="B45-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/14651858.CD010971.pub2" pmid="28072460" pmcid="PMC6464036" count="1">45</citation>,<citation rid="B75-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.5223/pghn.2022.25.5.376" pmid="36148289" pmcid="PMC9482830" count="1">75</citation>].

A major challenge remains the limited availability of high-quality pediatric studies. <sentence_start/>Compared with adults, children and adolescents are underrepresented in clinical trials investigating dietary interventions, microbiota-targeted therapies, circadian disruption, and psychological approaches. <sentence_start/>Many mechanistic insights regarding gut microbiota, intestinal permeability, and neuroendocrine pathways are derived from adult populations or experimental models, and their direct applicability to pediatric patients remains uncertain [<citation rid="B32-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/nu15122708" pmid="37375612" pmcid="PMC10302595" count="1">32</citation>,<citation rid="B33-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1080/17474124.2022.2055547" pmid="35311425" count="1">33</citation>,<citation rid="B38-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/jpepsy/jsad047" pmid="37515755" count="1">38</citation>,<citation rid="B42-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.2147/PHMT.S482343" pmcid="PMC11912920" pmid="40099110" count="1">42</citation>,<citation rid="B44-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1001/jamapediatrics.2022.0313" pmid="35404394" pmcid="PMC9002716" count="1">44</citation>,<citation rid="B45-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/14651858.CD010971.pub2" pmid="28072460" pmcid="PMC6464036" count="1">45</citation>,<citation rid="B67-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1002/14651858.CD012849.pub2" pmid="36799531" pmcid="PMC9945052" count="1">67</citation>,<citation rid="B69-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/nrgastro.2015.21" pmid="25666642" count="1">69</citation>].

Furthermore, determining the directionality of associations remains difficult. <sentence_start/>For example, it is unclear whether sleep disturbances and dietary irregularities contribute primarily to the development of gastrointestinal symptoms or whether chronic abdominal pain and altered bowel function lead to secondary changes in sleep, stress, and eating behaviors. <sentence_start/>Longitudinal studies are needed to clarify causal pathways and identify critical periods during childhood when lifestyle interventions may have the greatest preventive impact [<citation rid="B32-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/nu15122708" pmid="37375612" pmcid="PMC10302595" count="1">32</citation>,<citation rid="B33-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1080/17474124.2022.2055547" pmid="35311425" count="1">33</citation>,<citation rid="B38-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1093/jpepsy/jsad047" pmid="37515755" count="1">38</citation>,<citation rid="B42-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.2147/PHMT.S482343" pmcid="PMC11912920" pmid="40099110" count="1">42</citation>,<citation rid="B69-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1038/nrgastro.2015.21" pmid="25666642" count="1">69</citation>].

Finally, sleep, psychological stress, diet, and circadian behavior should not be considered independent exposures. <sentence_start/>Sleep timing affects meal timing and circadian alignment. <sentence_start/>Stress may affect both sleep and dietary behaviors, while the timing of food intake may, in turn, influence peripheral circadian rhythms and sleep [<citation rid="B34-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.1007/s11938-023-00433-1" count="1">34</citation>,<citation rid="B36-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3389/fendo.2023.1130689" pmcid="PMC10316519" pmid="37404311" count="1">36</citation>,<citation rid="B37-nutrients-18-02768" ref-type="bibr" doi="10.3390/nu15122743" pmid="37375647" pmcid="PMC10303702" count="1">37</citation>]. <sentence_start/>Consequently, conventional observational analyses may have difficulty separating direct effects from confounding, mediation, and interaction among these variables. <sentence_start/>Future prospective studies should therefore use repeated and, where possible, objective measurements of several lifestyle domains simultaneously and apply analytical approaches capable of evaluating their independent and combined effects.

Future research should focus on large-scale prospective pediatric cohorts using standardized diagnostic criteria, objective measures of sleep and circadian rhythms, validated dietary assessment tools, and integrated analysis of microbiome, immune, metabolic, and psychological parameters. <sentence_start/>Such studies are essential to develop personalized, evidence-based interventions targeting the gut-brain axis in children with DGBIs.
8. <sentence_start/>Conclusions

Pediatric disorders of gut-brain interaction (DGBIs) are common, clinically relevant conditions diagnosed primarily using symptom-based Rome criteria. <sentence_start/>Although the terminology and classification have evolved with Rome V, much of the pediatric evidence remains based on Rome III or Rome IV definitions. <sentence_start/>Across the available literature, sleep disturbance, psychological stress, and symptom-related functional impairment have the most consistent pediatric support, with associations involving abdominal pain, disability, quality of life, and school functioning. <sentence_start/>These relationships are bidirectional, as gastrointestinal symptoms may also disrupt sleep, daily functioning, and emotional well-being.

Several other mechanisms, including circadian misalignment, altered intestinal permeability, and microbiome-mediated gut-brain signaling, are biologically plausible but less firmly established in pediatric DGBIs. <sentence_start/>In particular, evidence linking social jetlag, meal timing, or sleep-related circadian disruption directly to specific pediatric DGBI outcomes remains limited, and much of the mechanistic evidence is derived from adult or experimental studies. <sentence_start/>Similarly, microbiome findings in children are heterogeneous and do not yet establish a consistent causal pathway.

From a clinical perspective, assessment should begin with an age-appropriate history and physical examination, including evaluation for alarm features. <sentence_start/>In children without alarm features whose symptoms are consistent with a DGBI, extensive routine investigations are generally not required, although targeted testing should be guided by the clinical phenotype and diagnostic uncertainty. <sentence_start/>Management should emphasize education, regular sleep and meal schedules, adequate hydration and fiber intake, physical activity, and individualized psychological or dietary support. <sentence_start/>Restrictive diets, including low-FODMAP approaches, should be reserved for selected patients and implemented with appropriate pediatric dietetic supervision.

Key research priorities include prospective pediatric studies using standardized diagnostic criteria and objective measures of sleep, circadian timing, and dietary intake, together with longitudinal assessment of microbiome, immune, metabolic, and psychological factors. <sentence_start/>Such studies are needed to clarify causality, identify clinically relevant subgroups, and determine whether targeting multiple modifiable lifestyle factors improves outcomes in pediatric DGBIs.
